Figurate Numbers in the Multiplication Table

AlgebraSequencesArithmetic
Game: A multiplication table lights up in different shapes, and the numbers in each shape add up to something surprising; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Move the pointer over the table (or press a cell, or use the arrow keys) and read the sum underneath. Pick a different shape with the buttons.

Shape
Look for the math

The multiplication table hides four identities. Each is a sum of table entries along a shape, and each equals a figurate number. The logic test summed the lit cells themselves for every n up to 300 and compared with the formulas.

Triangular squares and cubes

The sum of all entries of the n × n corner is (1 + 2 + … + n)² = [n(n+1)/2]²: the first row sums to n(n+1)/2, the second to twice that, and so on, so the total is (1 + 2 + … + n) · n(n+1)/2. The nth row and nth column together (the diagonal entry counted once) sum to 2n(1 + … + n) − n² = n² (n+1) − n² = n³. Adding such gnomons for 1, 2, …, n builds the square of the triangular number out of cubes: 1³ + 2³ + … + n³ = [n(n+1)/2]².

Squares

The diagonal of the table holds 1², 2², 3², …, and their sum is 1² + 2² + … + n² = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6.

Tetrahedral numbers

Add along an anti-diagonal: n·1 + (n−1)·2 + … + 1·n = n(n+1)(n+2)/6, the nth tetrahedral number, which counts the balls in a pyramid of n layers.

As in the applet, the table runs to 14 and the number n is the larger of the cell's column and row (for the anti-diagonal, column plus row minus 1).

Choose Cubes and move across the table. Which cell gives 7³ = 343?
